bib.title: Customer Relationship Management (Chapter 6, The Data Warehouse Toolkit)
bib.venue: book chapter, The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 2nd ed.

question: How should the customer dimension and related tables be designed in a dimensional data warehouse to support CRM analysis?
contributions: Customer name/address parsing and international handling
Common customer attributes: dates, segmentation scores, aggregated facts
Dimension outriggers for low-cardinality attribute clusters
Minidimensions for browsing, change tracking and variable-width attribute sets
Fixed-depth and variable-depth (bridge table) customer hierarchies
Consolidating customer data and querying across business processes

results.claim: A minidimension holds one row per unique combination of banded attributes; with 5 attributes of 10 values each it has 100,000 rows, which the authors give as a reasonable upper limit.

results.quote: then the demographics dimension could have 100,000 (105) rows. This is a reasonable upper limit for the number of rows in a minidimension.

results.claim: Bridge-table row count formula: multiply number of nodes at each level by the level depth and sum.

limits: Chapter assumes 2002-era relational DBMS and tools (Oracle CONNECT BY, nonrelational OLAP under 64,000 members); no empirical evaluation.
Band choices in a minidimension are hard to change later (authors concede).
Bridge tables are 'not for the faint of heart' and give overcounting risk; huge parts explosions may make the bridge enormous.
Examples are illustrative; no benchmark numbers for performance gains.
practices: Build a conformed customer dimension; do not let a packaged CRM application become a stovepipe data mart (p.145).
Parse names and addresses into elemental parts, then standardize and verify, rather than generic Name-1/Address-1 columns (p.147-148).
For international addresses, add a prebuilt address block attribute and several telephone dialing-sequence attributes, built once in staging (p.150).
Replace date attributes in the customer dimension with foreign keys to the date dimension, exposed as semantically distinct views (date outrigger) (p.151).
Store aggregated facts as customer attributes only for constraining and labeling, keep them few and slow-changing, and prefer descriptive bands like 'High Spender' (p.152).
Use a dimension outrigger only as an exception; many outriggers signal over-normalization (p.153).
For multimillion-row, rapidly changing customer dimensions, break frequently analyzed or changing attributes into a minidimension and avoid type 2 on the big table (p.154).
Convert continuous minidimension attributes (income, purchases) to banded ranges; keep raw values in the fact table if users need them (p.154-155).

Put both customer key and minidimension key in the fact table so the fact table records profile change; if the latest minidimension key is placed on the customer row, treat it as type 1 and label it current (p.155-156).
Cap a minidimension around 100,000 rows; split into several minidimensions (e.g. demographics vs purchase-credit scores), but never one per attribute (p.157).
Use a base dimension plus an extended-customer minidimension when prospects and customers have widely different attribute counts on fixed-width databases (p.158-159).

Use type 2 for customer dimensions under 100,000 rows and for very slowly changing leftover attributes; guard against overcounting with COUNT DISTINCT on the natural key or a most-recent-row indicator (p.159).
For point-in-time counts, constrain effective date <= date and expiration date >= date (operators depend on date rules) (p.160).
Capture keys of a query result as a behavior study group table and join to the customer natural key, hidden under a view (p.160-161).
Use denormalized level attributes for fixed-depth hierarchies, repeating lower-level values upward for shallow customers (p.162).

For ragged hierarchies use a bridge table, not a recursive pointer; constrain to one parent or use SELECT DISTINCT subsidiary keys to avoid double counting; add effective/expiration dates and weighting factors if needed (p.162-167).
Never join one dimension to two fact tables of different cardinality in one SELECT; use multipass SQL and outer join, or build a consolidated fact table (p.169-170).

terms.definition: a separate dimension of frequently analyzed or frequently changing attributes, with one row per unique combination of banded values, whose key is part of the fact table composite key
a dimension linked via a foreign key from another dimension; if the demographics key is a foreign key in the customer dimension it is an outrigger
a multimillion-row customer dimension whose attributes change often, making type 2 impractical
a physical table of customer keys captured from a query or exception report, used to constrain later analysis
a table between dimension and fact holding one row per pathway from a node to each subsidiary, plus a zero-length self row, with levels, bottom and top flags
removing low-cardinality columns of a dimension into separate normalized tables linked back to it
technique where a new row is added to the dimension table on change

code.snippet:
SELECT C.CUSTOMER_NAME, SUM(F.REVENUE)
FROM CUSTOMER C, BRIDGE B, FACT F, DATE D
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_KEY = B.PARENT_KEY
AND B.SUBSIDIARY_KEY = F.CUSTOMER_KEY
AND F.DATE_KEY = D.DATE_KEY
AND C.CUSTOMER_NAME = 'ABC General International'
AND D.MONTH = 'January 2002'
GROUP BY C.CUSTOMER_NAME

SELECT 'San Francisco', SUM(F.REVENUE)
FROM FACT F, DATE D
WHERE F.CUSTOMER_KEY IN 
(SELECT DISTINCT B.SUBSIDIARY_KEY
FROM CUSTOMER C, BRIDGE B
WHERE C.CUSTOMER_KEY = B.PARENT_KEY
AND C.CUSTOMER_CITY = 'San Francisco')
AND F.DATE_KEY = D.DATE_KEY
AND D.MONTH = 'January 2002'
GROUP BY 'San Francisco'
